elements.reason: The abstract does not report comparisons between groups or pooled comparative effects; the review focuses on prevalence/natural history and narrative synthesis, so group comparison direction is not applicable in the abstract.

elements.quote: the most frequent risks of bias for rcts concerned weaknesses in allocation concealment, blinding of therapists, and lack of intention-to-treat analysis. Most analytical studies failed to identify or deal with confounders, describe or deal with dropouts or eventually perform an appropriate statistical analysis .
elements.reason: The abstract briefly summarizes key limitations/risk of bias issues across included studies (issues in RCTs and analytical observational studies).

elements.quote: conclusions: Most studies in this updated review targeted the prevalence of limitations of functioning of rehabilitation interest in coVID-19 survivors. ... More rcts and analytical observational studies are available, but the methodological quality of recently published studies is low. There is a need for good quality intervention efficacy and effectiveness studies to complement the rapidly expanding evidence from observational studies.
elements.reason: The abstract provides an interpretation of the findings and the implications for future research and practice.
The abstract does not report the primary source of funding for the review.
The abstract does not provide a registry name or registration number (PROSPERO registration is reported elsewhere in the paper but not in the abstract).

elements.quote: A high proportion of SARS-CoV-2 patients survive infection but the prevalence of chronic sequelae and resulting disability is increasing. These survivors need clinical management and rehabilitation to facilitate good health outcomes. The best available research evidence is required to inform management and rehabilitation decisions, interventions, and health systems for COVID-19 survivors with adverse clinical sequelae. Further evidence is warranted to estimate the resources needed to plan for setting appropriate and adequately delivered post-acute and long-term rehabilitation services.
elements.reason: Explicit description of the current state (increasing prevalence of chronic sequelae, survivors' needs) and identification of important uncertainties/gaps (need for evidence to inform management, resource estimation, and rehabilitation services).

elements.quote: The best available research evidence is required to inform management and rehabilitation decisions, interventions, and health systems for COVID-19 survivors with adverse clinical sequelae. Further evidence is warranted to estimate the resources needed to plan for setting appropriate and adequately delivered post-acute and long-term rehabilitation services.
elements.reason: The manuscript states the importance and need for the review: to provide best-available evidence to inform clinical management, interventions, health systems, and resource planning for rehabilitation of COVID-19 survivors.

elements.quote: The methodology of this systematic review updates the second edition published in June 2020. It follows the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) Guidelines ... The protocol has been updated in PROSPERO (CRD42021181202). ... The search strategy, screening, and data extraction criteria were not changed from the previous edition except for the exclusion of case reports and case series.
elements.reason: The authors explicitly state this edition updates prior editions (including a second edition) and reference updating the protocol in PROSPERO, explaining how the current review relates to and modifies previous reviews.

No text in the provided evidence describes a proposed mechanism of action for rehabilitation interventions; while some included studies report intervention effectiveness, the review does not present a brief mechanism of action.
No evidence in the provided text indicates that a logic model was considered or presented for complex interventions or delivery contexts.

elements.quote: introduction: this paper updates and summarizes the current evidence informing rehabilitation of patients with coVid-19 and/or describing the consequences of the disease and its treatment.
elements.reason: An explicit objective is stated (to update and summarize evidence on rehabilitation and consequences of COVID-19), but it is not framed using a recognized question-formulation framework (eg, PICO or similar).
Although the review includes intervention studies (noted in text_6 and text_2), there is no explicit statement of planned comparisons using PICO or an appropriate variant in the provided evidence.

elements.quote: The database search was conducted on July 2 nd , 2021 covering publication dates between May 1st and June 30 th , 2021.
elements.reason: Explicit statement of the date the database search was conducted (July 2, 2021) and coverage dates for publications.
No bibliographic database names, search interfaces/platforms, or coverage dates for each database are reported in the provided evidence.
No study registers, regulatory databases, or online repositories searched are named nor are date restrictions for such sources reported.

elements.quote: New studies were added to the consolidated online table of papers of all editions and to the interactive living evidence map available on the Cochrane Rehabilitation REH-COVER action website (https://tr.im/rr_dyn).
elements.reason: A website URL is reported for the interactive living evidence map, but the text does not explicitly state this website was searched as an information source or provide details for each website/search engine used.
No organisations or manufacturers contacted to identify studies are named in the provided evidence.
No description of types of individuals contacted to identify studies is provided in the evidence.
No information is given about the types of reference lists examined.
No details on backward or forward citation searching (seed reports, citation index/platform, or search date) are reported in the provided evidence.
No journals or conference proceedings consulted are named, nor are dates covered or search methods for such sources reported.

No complete search strategies or search strings for individual databases, registers, or websites are reported in the provided evidence. The text only states the date of the database search and that the search strategy was unchanged from a prior edition, but does not present the actual search strings.

elements.quote: "The database search was conducted on July 2nd, 2021 covering publication dates between May 1st and June 30th, 2021."
elements.reason: A date limit for the search is reported. Additionally, exclusion of case reports and case series is noted elsewhere (text_6 and text_15) with a rationale to narrow breadth and increase evidence level, but full description and justification of all search limits by reference to eligibility criteria is incomplete.

elements.quote: "The search strategy, screening, and data extraction criteria were not changed from the previous edition 4 except for the exclusion of case reports and case series."
elements.reason: The manuscript cites the previous edition as the source of the search strategy and explicitly states the current strategy was unchanged except for a specified exclusion, which constitutes citation of a published approach and description of an adaptation.
No mention of natural-language processing or text-analysis tools used to identify or refine search terms is present in the retrieved evidence.
No information about tools used to translate search strings between sources is reported in the provided evidence.
The evidence contains no description of validation of the search strategy or any validation studies/processes.
There is no description of any peer review of the search strategy (e.g., PRESS) in the retrieved text.
No information is provided about the conceptual structure of the search or whether the search was based on PICO; therefore no description of alternative structure or its development is present.
No information is provided specifying how many reviewers screened records or full reports at each screening stage; retrieved chunks mention screening occurred but do not report numbers of reviewers.

There is no explicit statement about whether reviewers worked independently at title/abstract or full-text screening stages. The only independence statement refers to two authors appraising quality, not to screening.

No description of processes used to resolve screening disagreements is provided. The text describes resolution of disagreements for quality appraisal (consensus and third author) but does not state how screening disagreements were resolved.
No processes are described for obtaining or confirming eligibility information from study investigators in the retrieved evidence.
The retrieved text does not report any methods used to translate abstracts or full articles for eligibility assessment.
There is no description of integration of automation tools into the selection process in the provided evidence.
No information is provided identifying externally derived classifiers, their role, or records removed before screening.
The manuscript does not report use, training, or validation of internally derived classifiers in the selection process.
There is no description of machine-learning prioritisation tools or stopping/prioritisation rules for screening in the retrieved evidence.
No mention is made of crowdsourcing platforms or their integration into study selection.
The document does not describe previously screened datasets used to eliminate records or how such datasets were derived.
No explicit statement reporting the number of reviewers who collected data from each report (no text specifying how many reviewers performed data extraction).
No explicit statement indicating whether multiple data collectors worked independently during data collection/extraction.

No explicit description of processes used to resolve disagreements between data collectors for data extraction (only processes for quality appraisal disagreements are described, not for data collection).
No information on processes used to obtain or confirm data from study investigators is reported in the provided evidence.
No description of any automation tools used for data collection (use, training, validation) is present in the retrieved evidence.
No methods for translating articles for data collection are reported in the provided text.
No software specified for extracting data from figures is reported in the retrieved evidence.

elements.quote: "Additionally, to manage discrepancies encountered in past editions between the study design declared by the authors and the actual design of the study, we classified study designs according to the Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality 7 (Supplementary Digital Material 1: Supplementary Text File 1)."
elements.reason: The authors report a specific rule for handling discrepancies in study design by classifying designs according to AHRQ guidance, which addresses resolving one type of inconsistency across reports; however, broader decision rules for selecting among multiple reports or resolving other types of inconsistent data are not described.

elements.quote: Table I, II, and III synthesize the distribution of selected studies by geographical area (Table I), limitations of functioning of rehabilitation interest (LFRI), disease phase and rehabilitation setting (Table II), research question, and study design (Table III).
elements.reason: The manuscript explicitly reports the concept of 'limitations of functioning of rehabilitation interest (LFRI)' and categorizes studies by research question (e.g. prevalence, natural history, intervention effectiveness), but it does not provide a comprehensive list and formal definitions of all outcome domains sought.

elements.quote: All study participants were COVID survivors and 48% of studies collected information on participants 6 months or longer after COVID-19 onset.
elements.reason: The review reports follow-up timeframes for the included studies (e.g. 6 months or longer, up to one year in other sections), but it does not specify the time frame of measurement separately for each outcome domain.
There is no explicit statement indicating whether the review sought all results compatible with each outcome domain (for all measures, time points, analyses) or not.

The manuscript does not describe any process used to select among multiple compatible results within outcome domains (there is no method described for choosing measures, time points, or analyses when multiple were available).

elements.quote: The protocol has been updated in PROSPERO (CRD42021181202). ... The search strategy, screening, and data extraction criteria were not changed from the previous edition 4 except for the exclusion of case reports and case series.
elements.reason: While the protocol update and a change excluding case reports/series are reported, there is no report of changes to outcome-domain inclusion, definitions, or their relative importance with rationales; thus changes to outcomes are not documented.
The manuscript does not report any changes to processes for selecting results within eligible outcome domains nor provide rationales for such changes.
The review does not report which outcomes were considered most important for interpreting the conclusions nor the rationale for prioritizing them.

elements.quote: papers were categorized according to study design, research question, coVid-19 phase, limitations of functioning of rehabilitation interest, and type of rehabilitation service involved.
elements.reason: The manuscript explicitly lists multiple variables that were collected (study design, research question, COVID-19 phase, LFRI, type of rehabilitation service). However, the retrieved evidence does not provide definitions for these variables or a comprehensive list of all 'other variables' sought (e.g., participant characteristics, funding sources) nor formal definitions, so the requirement is only partially met.

No explicit description of assumptions made about missing or unclear study information is present in the supplied evidence. The text mentions classifying study design to manage discrepancies (text_6) but does not describe assumptions regarding missing or unclear data.

elements.quote: It follows the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) Guidelines 5 and the Interim Guidance from the Cochrane Rapid Reviews Methods Group. 6 The protocol has been updated in PROSPERO (CRD42021181202).
elements.reason: The authors cite PRISMA and Cochrane Rapid Reviews interim guidance and register a protocol in PROSPERO, which serve as referenced tools/guidance informing the review methods and the approach to data collection; thus a tool/guidance used to determine which data items to collect is cited.

elements.quote: from this edition, we improved the quality assessment using the Joanna briggs institute checklists for observational studies and the cochrane risk of bias tool for randomized-controlled clinical trials (rcts).
elements.reason: The manuscript names the tools used (Joanna Briggs Institute checklists for observational studies and the Cochrane Risk of Bias tool for RCTs). However, a version or detailed version identifier is only explicitly indicated for the Cochrane tool as 'RoB 1' elsewhere; the JBI checklist version is not specified, so the element is only partially met.

elements.quote: Figure 2.-Distribution of Risks of Bias in the included Randomized Controlled trials, according to the Cochrane Risk of Bias (RoB 1) tool.
elements.reason: The Cochrane RoB 1 domains are explicitly shown in the provided Figure 2 (chunk_id text_8 image): visible domain labels include 'Generation of allocation sequence', 'Allocation concealment', 'Blinding of participants', 'Blinding of personnel/care providers (performance bias)', 'Blinding of outcome assessor (detection bias)', 'Incomplete outcome data (attrition bias)', 'Selective reporting (reporting bias)', and two 'Other bias' items (e.g. 'Group similarity at baseline', 'intention-to-treat analysis'). However, the specific domains/items assessed by the JBI checklists are not listed in the text, so only partial specification is provided.
No explicit statement reports whether an overall risk-of-bias judgement per study was made or the rules/criteria used to derive any overall judgements.
There is no description in the retrieved evidence of any adaptations made to existing risk-of-bias tools.

The manuscript reports using established tools (JBI checklists and Cochrane RoB 1) and does not indicate development of any new risk-of-bias tool; thus the item about newly developed tools is not applicable.

elements.quote: Two review authors (C.A., V.I.) independently appraised the quality of studies and resolved disagreements by consensus; in the case of persistent disagreement, a third review author was consulted (P.C.) and the disagreement resolved by consensus.
elements.reason: The manuscript clearly states the number of reviewers (two), that they worked independently, and the procedure for resolving disagreements including consulting a third author if needed.
No information is provided about processes used to obtain or confirm risk-of-bias information from study investigators.
The manuscript does not describe the use of any automation tools for risk-of-bias assessment (use, training, performance, or validation). There is no explicit statement that such tools were not used.

The manuscript does not specify, for any outcome or outcome type, which effect measure(s) (e.g. risk ratio, mean difference) were used in synthesis or presentation. No methods or results text indicate effect measures.
No effect measures are reported anywhere in the provided evidence; therefore reporting thresholds or ranges used to interpret effect sizes does not apply.
No synthesized results or effect measures are reported in the provided evidence, so methods to re-express results using another effect measure are not applicable.
The manuscript does not state any choice of effect measure in the provided evidence, so there is nothing to justify regarding effect-measure choice.

elements.quote: Table I, II, and III synthesize the distribution of selected studies by geographical area (Table I), limitations of functioning of rehabilitation interest (LFRI), disease phase and rehabilitation setting (Table II), research question, and study design (Table III).
elements.reason: The manuscript reports that included studies were categorized and summarized in tables by study characteristics (research question, study design, disease phase, LFRI, etc.), indicating some process of grouping studies for synthesis. However, it does not provide detailed processes used to decide which studies were eligible for each specific synthesis (e.g., explicit rules or procedures comparing study intervention characteristics against planned synthesis groups), so the reporting is incomplete.

The provided evidence describes study selection, classification, quality appraisal, and that a narrative synthesis and tables were used (text_5, text_6, text_7, table_2), but contains no description of methods to prepare data for presentation or synthesis (e.g., handling missing summary statistics, data conversions, imputation, or transformation). No verbatim text on these procedures is present in the retrieved evidence.

elements.quote: This rapid living systematic review of LFRI experienced by COVID-19 patients confirms the important impact of the disease on rehabilitation needs. The information gap about the course of functional recovery after the resolution of symptoms in people with and without complications is being filled by the increasing number of studies reporting on outcomes 6-12 month after COVID-19 onset. However, we still lack high-quality studies reporting on the efficacy and effectiveness of rehabilitation at the individual level, but more importantly at the service and system levels. The literature search was comprehensive with the search strategy replicating previous review editions that, to date, have been the most complete investigations of rehabilitation evidence related to COVID in health literature. In this third edition, one modification was introduced to the selection criteria to narrow the breadth of findings and increase the level of evidence sought by excluding case reports and case series. From a content point of view, it was clear that there was saturation of evidence on the clinical description of COVID-19 survivors in the literature - our clinical information need was about prevalence, natural history, and interventions. The applicability of findings was not affected by this change. Further, the use of a proven search strategy, screening, and interpretation of findings by a multidisciplinary rehabilitation team also support applicability to the clinical information need.
elements.reason: The authors explicitly compare the current findings to prior review editions and to the broader literature, note where evidence is increasing (longer follow-up studies) and where gaps remain (lack of high-quality intervention studies), thus interpreting results in the context of other evidence.
